documents.title: Academic Integrity and Syllabus Support in the Age of Generative AI
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors that 'Instructors must create explicit policies outlining when AI tools can be used', says 'you can establish different AI policies for each assignment', and supplies sample statements ranging from permissive to prohibitive, while advising 'Instead of banning AI'. It sets no single school rule, so the decision is handed to instructors.
tiers: AI in Writing and Research Assignments

documents.summary: A Steinhardt AI Hub page that advises faculty to write explicit AI statements and offers sample syllabus language for permitted use, prohibited use, attribution, group work and art or music reflections. It also covers student-data privacy under FERPA, assessment design, citation formats for AI, and a notice that detectors are unreliable. It is school-level and not specific to computing.

documents.stance_why: The guide says AI use 'is not cheating if a faculty member approves its use in a class assignment' and that students should 'clarify the extent of the use of AI tools in specific classes and assignments'; unapproved use risks violating the Academic Integrity Policy. It sets no uniform rule and defers to faculty.
documents.summary: A library research guide that quotes NYU's Academic Integrity Policy definition of cheating and says AI use depends on faculty approval. It lists NYU's licensed AI services, notes Turnitin AI detection is disabled and unreliable, and gives advice on evaluating and citing AI text. It is a library guide, not an official policy page.

notes: Official www.nyu.edu university AI pages were inaccessible (bot challenge), so the university layer here is the NYU Libraries guide only. No computing-unit policy found. Steinhardt is a non-computing school; its page is guidance with sample statements, so many units are sample or template language addressed to instructors.
